DOCUMENT:
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%" -- The hotel is described as a 112-room hotel in the Context section, but the revenue estimate uses 124 rooms. With 112 rooms the same calculation gives 112 x 104 x 0.79 x £20 = about £184,000, not £204,000.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels" -- The only evidence is that occupancy rose from June to July after a June rate rise, but the document itself says July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. The seasonal rise confounds the comparison; it cannot show demand is price-insensitive (let alone that the higher price helped).
3. [missing_consideration] at: "We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above." -- The document states that about 38% of Saturday-night bookings are wedding guests from the adjacent venue who stay only Saturday night. A two-night minimum would exclude or deter this group, but the revenue case assumes occupancy is maintained and never addresses the loss of these single-night Saturday bookings.

REVIEW:
# Review: Weekend Rate Restructure proposal

The conclusion that the hotel is underpriced may well be right, but the document does not support the claim that this is a well-evidenced, low-risk change. The central evidence is confounded, the headline figure is overstated and not a floor, and the two-night minimum is under-examined.

## 1. The price-sensitivity "test" is not a test (most serious)
- **Seasonality is the obvious explanation.** The rise from 81% (June) to 89% (July) coincides with the harbour festival and school holidays, which the document itself names as the drivers of July and August strength. Table 1 shows occupancy climbing into summer anyway. There is no control, such as a comparison with July 2024 or with competitors' June-to-July movement, so the effect of the £10 rise can't be isolated.
- **The rise took effect in the last week of June**, so June is essentially all old-rate and July all new-rate. This makes the comparison a seasonal one.
- **The conclusion is over-extended.** "Guests are not price sensitive" and "reinforced our positioning as a quality option" are asserted, not shown. At best, a 7% rise did not visibly cause a collapse in a peak month.
- **The proposed increase is twice as large** (£20, about 14%) and applies year-round. Evidence from peak July says little about January (62%), February (66%) or November (72%), where demand is softer and price sensitivity is likely higher.
- **Constrained inventory hides elasticity.** With 31 Saturday sell-outs, observed occupancy on those nights can't show demand response. That points to underpricing on peak Saturdays, not to Fridays or off-peak weekends having headroom.

## 2. The £204,000 figure is overstated and is not a floor
- **Room count inconsistency.** Section 2 says 112 rooms, Section 5 uses 124. 124 × 104 × 79% × £20 ≈ £204k, but with 112 rooms it is about £184k. That is roughly £20k, or 10%, overstated.
- **It assumes every occupied room pays BAR.** Corporate contracted rates, group rates and wedding blocks are excluded from the increase (Section 6), and those are likely a large share of weekend volume. Other discounted or non-BAR channels are not addressed. OTA commission and VAT (if the £20 is gross) would also reduce net revenue.
- **"No occupancy loss" is the optimistic assumption, not a conservative one.** The estimate assumes zero volume response to a 14% rise. Break-even is about 69% occupancy (£145 × 79% ≈ £165 × 69.4%), so there is cushion, but the figure is a best case for volume, not a floor.
- **The two-night minimum is not purely upside.** It also loses revenue where it turns away one-night Saturday guests, and that loss is not netted off. The claim that extra Friday and Sunday revenue "should be material" is unquantified, and Sunday is outside the weekend BAR.
- **The recommendation says "at least £204,000"**, which the above does not support.

## 3. The two-night minimum may hit the wedding business
- Weddings at Quayside Hall account for about 38% of Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically arrive Saturday and leave Sunday morning, so they are exactly the one-night stays the minimum would block or push elsewhere.
- The document doesn't say whether wedding blocks are exempt. "Contracted group rates will be honoured" covers only what is already contracted. Blocks booked through the couple, and future wedding business, may not be covered.
- Losing even a fraction of 38% of Saturday demand on the hotel's most constrained night could outweigh the added Friday and Sunday nights. The proposal needs the actual share of Saturday stays that are one-night, and how many are wedding-related.
- The minimum also risks reputational damage with the neighbouring venue, which is a source of repeat business.

## 4. The value-for-money score cuts the other way
- A score of 8.4, the best in the set, was achieved at a price £20–£35 below competitors. It is probably partly a result of the low price, so it will likely fall after a 14% rise.
- Survey respondents are people who stayed, so the score tells us nothing about guests who were deterred.
- The document gives no evidence of the scores of the comparator hotels on quality, only on value.

## 5. Competitive positioning is thinly evidenced
- Only three comparator hotels are cited, with a rate range and no detail on their quality, facilities or location.
- A £20 rise puts Harbourside at £165, equal to the cheapest competitor. Competitors may also raise rates, or discount, in response or in the same period. Their occupancy is not given.
- "Occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023" has no supporting data.

## 6. Monitoring is weaker than described
- The trigger only says the rate will be "reviewed", with no commitment to revert or adjust, no owner and no deadline.
- A monthly occupancy threshold lags. By the time a month closes, a further month of bookings is on the books.
- Comparing against 2025 is distorted by that year's mid-year £10 rise, and occupancy alone ignores ADR and RevPAR, which is what actually matters. A better trigger would use RevPAR and pick-up pace, and would be set per season.
- Forward bookings at the old £145 rate for peak summer may already be on the books, so early occupancy will look healthy and mask any demand effect.
- Two weeks' notice to OTAs is short, and the document doesn't address how already-taken bookings are treated.

## 7. Suggestions
1. Rebuild the price-sensitivity evidence with year-on-year comparisons (July 2025 vs July 2024, adjusted for the festival and holidays) and competitor movement over the same period.
2. Fix the room count and recompute the revenue estimate on BAR-paying room nights only, with scenarios for occupancy loss of 0, 3, 5 and 8 points, net of commission and VAT.
3. Quantify the two-night minimum, covering the one-night Saturday share, the wedding share, and the Friday/Sunday fill rate actually achievable. Consider exempting weddings or applying the minimum only to peak Saturdays.
4. Consider a seasonal or tiered increase (larger in July–September, smaller or none in January–March) and a smaller first step, for example £10–£15.
5. Define a stronger monitoring and rollback mechanism with RevPAR-based triggers, an owner and a time limit.
6. Reword the recommendation and the author's summary. "Evidence shows guests are not price sensitive" and "£204,000 is a floor" are not supported by the document.
